h1:
Sing Buri Boat Noodles
8 Tiny Bowls of Rich, Dark Broth
intro: Mention Sing Buri and a lot of people think of Mae La snakehead fish first, but the food nearly every car on the Asia Highway pulls over for is boat noodles — tiny bowls of dark, intense broth packed with offal, ordered three or four at a time and paid for by the bowl. These are the shops locals genuinely eat at, with areas, hours and rough prices.
chips: 🍜 Tiny bowls, pay by the count

blocks.html: Sing Buri boat noodles aren't about one famous shop — they're spread across several areas: along the Asia Highway (Route 32), where passing cars stop easily; on the Sing Buri–Bang Rachan road, where locals drive out to eat; and at small shops in town. What they share is the small bowl, a dark broth that runs sweet from blood, offal and meatballs, and a tab counted by how many bowls you stack up. We picked 8 shops that are open and have real reviews behind them.

blocks.text: What are Sing Buri boat noodles, and why the tiny bowls?

blocks.html: Boat noodles were originally sold from boats in the canals, so the bowls were made small — quick to finish and easy to pass around on a rocking boat. When the trade moved onto dry land the small bowl stuck. The broth is cooked richer than ordinary noodles, with fresh blood stirred in to make it thick and savory-sweet, so diners order several bowls at a time. In Sing Buri many shops still tally the bill by counting the bowls stacked on your table.

blocks.title: How to eat like a local
blocks.html: Start with 3 bowls per person and top up from there, because the bowls really are small · fried sides like crispy pork rind or fried chicken skin usually sit on the table for you to grab, charged by what you eat · if you like the broth thick, ask for extra blood.

blocks.text: 8 boat noodle shops Sing Buri locals go to

items.name: Lan Mae Phayung Boat Noodles
items.blurb: A roadside shop on the Asia Highway where travelers stop to fill up. The broth is bold and old-school, the bowls loaded with meatballs, fresh pork, liver, intestine and heart. Plenty of people name it the first stop that comes to mind when you say Sing Buri boat noodles.
items.meta: On the Asia Highway · open daily 08.00–16.00

items.name: Tor Tor Boat Noodles
items.blurb: On the Sing Buri–Bang Rachan road, about 300 m past the Wat Budda (Luang Tia) junction, on your left. Locals drive out here a lot. There's braised-pork and braised-beef boat noodles plus a spicy nam tok version, and the price is easy to keep in check.
items.meta: Sing Buri–Bang Rachan road · open daily 09.30–15.30

items.name: Heng Heng Boat Noodles (Ton Pho)
items.blurb: A homey roadside shop, with the bodhi tree (ton pho) as the landmark. Very easy on the wallet, starting at just over ten baht a bowl — good for a quick stop along the way. Locals nearby eat here all the time.
items.meta: In Sing Buri town, near the bodhi tree

items.name: Tiao Ruea Yutya (Asia Highway branch, next to Makro)
items.blurb: A boat noodle branch that's easy to pull into on the Asia Highway, right next to Makro Sing Buri. Good for drivers passing through who want a quick stop, with easy parking, a well-balanced broth and the full set of toppings.

items.name: Mueang Sing Boat Noodles
items.blurb: An in-town shop with a steady stream of reviews, focused on the traditional small-bowl boat noodles with a rich broth, eaten alongside fried sides. Handy if you don't want to head far outside town.

items.name: Sala Thai Boat Noodles
items.blurb: A shop that still charges the old way — a regular bowl starts in the low double digits, and a special is only a little more. Good for a tight budget when you want to put away several bowls of proper boat noodles.

items.name: Saep Sadet Boat Noodles (Sing Buri branch)
items.blurb: A rich, well-rounded broth that plenty of people say is good enough without adding any seasoning. This branch is easy to find in town — a solid pick if you like a bold broth.

items.name: Tom Yum Snakehead Fish Noodles (past Wat Amphawan)
items.blurb: Not boat noodles with pork blood exactly, but a thick tom yum noodle soup with fresh snakehead fish. It's about 2 km past Wat Amphawan — good if you want a punchy bowl that works in one of Sing Buri's best ingredients, the snakehead fish.

blocks.text: Which area should you stop to eat in?

items: Along the Asia Highway (Route 32) — the easiest option for anyone driving through: simple parking, a quick stop, a good place to fill up on the way north.
Sing Buri–Bang Rachan road — the route locals drive out to eat on, a quiet rural feel and prices that are easy to keep down.
In Sing Buri town — good if you're staying in town or strolling along the Chao Phraya River; easy to find a shop on foot.

blocks.title: A note on timing
blocks.html: Most boat noodle shops are daytime spots, open from morning into the afternoon, with many closing around 15.30–16.00. If you've got your heart set on a particular shop, get there before 2 pm to be safe, and check the shop's page on the day you plan to go — small shops can close on random days.

Because the bowls are small, most people order 3–5 per meal, working out to around 60–100 THB per person including fried sides and a drink. At the budget-friendly shops like Sala Thai or Heng Heng you can eat your fill for under sixty — a roadside meal that's good value and easy to linger over with the family.

items.name: Eat it with fried sides
items.blurb: Crispy pork rind, fried chicken skin and pork crackling sit on the table for you to grab, charged by what you eat — they cut through the thick broth nicely.

items.name: Finish with dessert
items.blurb: Several areas have Thai sweet shops and shaved-ice stalls nearby, an easy next stop once you've had your fill of noodles.

faq.q: Which Sing Buri boat noodle shop do locals go to most?
faq.a: Lan Mae Phayung on the Asia Highway gets the most talk among travelers, while locals on the Bang Rachan side often head to Tor Tor Boat Noodles on the Sing Buri–Bang Rachan road. Both have a rich broth and bowls packed with toppings.

faq.q: How much per bowl, and how many do I need to feel full?
faq.a: Most are around 15–20 THB a bowl, and a few that still charge the old way start at 10 THB. Since the bowls are small, most people order 3–5 per meal, working out to about 60–100 THB per person including fried sides.

faq.q: What time do Sing Buri boat noodle shops open?
faq.a: Most are daytime shops, opening in the morning around 08.00–09.30 and closing in the afternoon around 15.30–16.00. Go before 2 pm and check the shop's page first, since small shops can close on random days.

faq.q: Can I stop for a bowl while driving through?
faq.a: Easily. Roadside shops on the Asia Highway like Lan Mae Phayung and Tiao Ruea Yutya next to Makro have simple parking — a good place to fill up on the way north.

faq.q: How are boat noodles different from regular noodles?
faq.a: The bowls are much smaller, the broth is cooked richer with fresh blood stirred in to make it thick and savory-sweet, it usually comes with offal and meatballs, and you're charged by counting the bowls you eat.
